newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lyonnaise, Suez up on deal talk.
newsitem.headline: Lyonnaise, Suez up on deal talk.

text.p: Shares in French water utility Lyonnaise des Eaux and holding company Cie de Suez rose sharply in early trading on Monday due to persistent reports of a merger deal to be drafted by the end of the month.

Lyonnaise shares were up 2.14 percent and Suez shares up 1.64 percent as of 1140 GMT in a declining market after a weekend report that the two firms' chairmen hoped to draft a merger plan for presenting to an April 1 Suez board meeting.

Both companies refused to comment on a report in Saturday's Le Monde newspaper that Lyonnaise chairman Jerome Monod and Lyonnaise chairman Gerard Mestrallet were spending the weekend working on a merger deal.
"The market is no longer wondering whether it will happen but when and at what terms," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Jean-Baptiste Bellon.
Glassmaker Saint Gobain, whose chairman Jean-Louis Beffa was said by Le Monde to be involved in the talks, also had no comment, a spokeswoman said.
But market rumours that a deal was in the works gained credibility last week when Etienne Davignon, chairman of Suez unit Societe Generale de Belgique SA, acknowledged that a merger was possible.
However, he said no decision had been made and the idea had not been presented to the board.
Suez already owns 16.8 percent of Lyonnaise. Saint-Gobain holds a little over six percent of Suez's capital and 10 percent of the voting rights.
Analysts said the deal would make sense for Suez which has lost its raison d'etre after having sold off most of its assets including its crown jewel Banque Indosuez.
The big attraction for Lyonnaise, on the other hand, would be Suez's cash hoard and its handful of industrial holdings.
Lyonnaise, whose main businesses are water contracts, construction and energy, has high hopes for global expansion but lacks the resources to finance growth, the analysts said.
The possibility of a merger pact has worried Lyonnaise's chief competitor Compagnie Generale des Eaux. It fears the combination would produce not a bigger rival but a financially stronger one.

Compagnie Generale des Eaux has said a merger would harm Suez's minority shareholders but denied a report in the Financial weekly Investir that it was considering a hostile bid for Suez to block any pact.

Talk of a merger has also worried Belgian officials who fear that a deal would leave Tractebel, a utility group indirectly controlled by Suez which is Belgium's principal supplier of electricity, under French control.

Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene has voiced concern that a merger might harm Brussels's interests. He is already angry with Paris about French carmaker Renault SA's decision to close its Vilvoorde assembly plant near Brussels, threatening 3,100 Belgian jobs.
Le Monde, however, said it appeared that Dehaene had been offered assurances on Tractebel's autonomy following a merger.
One investment banker said Suez's financial strength was in any case more important to the success of an eventual merger than industrial synergies between Tractebel and Lyonnaise.

Deutsche Morgan's Bellon said any merger was likely to be structured to allow Suez to bid for the shares of Lyonnaise. Suez is the larger firm and has cash and important unused tax losses which would be lost if it were acquired by Lyonnaise.
